extracted.intended_audience: early-career academic researchers and NIH grant applicants (PIs, postdocs preparing to apply), research community following NIH funding policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative expectations about how often and in what manner to submit NIH grant applications (especially R01s) for early-career PIs, including timelines, revised applications, and how programmatic/ESI/FOA rules affect multiple awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission volume / probabilistic approach (apply until funded)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only way to beat the odds at NIH is to submit a lot of grant applications... this is a probabilistic endeavor. Some who put in a lot of grant applications over a period of several years are going to come up empty. Some who put in a lot of applications will land one grant. And some, inevitably will end up with more than one grant funded."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended behavior: persistent, repeated submission is appropriate and expected. Treat funding as probabilistic rather than proof of merit per single submission. Anti-pattern: blaming a PI for submitting many applications or labeling them as 'greedy' for eventual multiple awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical new-PI submission timeline and concurrency of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative example of an Assistant Professor who submits multiple new R01s and amended applications across review cycles (e.g., first R01 Oct 2022, additional submissions Feb/June/Oct 2023; amended proposals in July/Nov 2023), resulting in several applications in flight without scores for long periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret multiple concurrent applications as a normal, sometimes necessary pattern for an ESI trying to establish funding. Expect many months of pending applications, staggered reviews, and overlapping score outcomes. Do not view multiple applications in cycle as evidence of malfeasance without score/award context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amended (revised/resubmitted) applications are easier and strategically appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Trust me, those amended proposals are a lot easier to do." Amended proposals (revisions) are often lighter work than brand-new proposals and are frequently submitted in subsequent cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: revise and resubmit rather than only producing brand-new applications; amended submissions are a practical way to keep applications in the pipeline and should not be stigmatized. Anti-pattern: cancelling or pulling reasonable amendments prematurely merely because others view volume as problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI policy can legitimately lead to multiple awards to the same early-career investigator
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is ESI policy to consider. Depending on the IC this can be a big help. And I’ve seen situations where the POs sort of conveniently ignore another pending application and basically give the ESI boost twice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should account for ESI (Early Stage Investigator) policies: program officers may apply ESI considerations or programmatic priority in ways that result in multiple awards to the same investigator, including across ICs. This is policy-driven, not necessarily evidence of 'greed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted funding opportunities and programmatic priorities affect award decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: If one or more applications were submitted for a targeted FOA, they may be picked up for that reason; programmatic interest and targeted FOAs can cause certain proposals to be funded even if other scores are close to payline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that funding decisions are not determined solely by summary score percentiles; FOA alignment and program priorities can create legitimate exceptions. When evaluating fairness, consider whether FOAs or programmatic goals explain multiple awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge funding fairness without knowing scores, paylines, or Notice of Award (NoA)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Without knowing any of the scores... we don’t know what Program was doing... Certainly before there was a NoA which is the real finish line."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assess whether multiple awards are unfair, you need concrete information: summary scores, percentiles, paylines, and whether Notices of Award were issued. Anti-pattern: public outrage or accusations absent these data points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable/typical PI effort percentages on awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Effort norms cited: "50% for the first two would not raise any eyebrows at all. 33%? no biggie. Even 25% is seemingly normal. And for established PIs, 20% effort is likewise normal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether workload/effort on multiple grants is appropriate, use these common benchmarks as context. Different institutions and fields may vary, but these percentages are presented as typical and acceptable in NIH-funded labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative timing, program officer/IC actions, and document finalization make it hard to withdraw awards
rubrics_metrics.description: By the time Grants Management Officials (GMOs) are finalizing documents and Program Officers of multiple ICs realize awards are about to be loaded on a lab, it becomes "too hard to then pull the plug." Awards may have staggered start dates (April/May/June) and admin delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical realities—contracting, OSs, GMOs, and inter-IC coordination—mean that once multiple awards start progressing, administrative inertia can lead to concurrent awards. This explains how an early-career PI might legitimately have multiple overlapping grants.
